SPACEX MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST STARSHIP UPPER-STAGE TOWER CATCH

Ship 42 returned from orbit and was caught by the launch tower arms at Starbase around 4:20 p.m. ET, roughly 22.5 hours after liftoff.

SpaceX had planned to catch both stages, but the Super Heavy booster was diverted offshore after its catch was aborted.

zh_summary: Explains Starship’s plasma blackout and why SpaceX lands it with engines instead of parachutes for Mars, quoting Kate Tice on reentry.
en_summary: Explains Starship’s plasma blackout and why SpaceX lands it with engines instead of parachutes for Mars, quoting Kate Tice on reentry.
text:
Starship’s plasma blackout explained, and why SpaceX lands it with engines instead of parachutes for Mars:

Kate Tice: “Reentry is typically a portion of flight where we don’t have communications with the spacecraft, because it’s reentering at or around orbital velocity. That’s roughly eight kilometers per second, or about five miles per second. And at those speeds, the spacecraft is moving through the atmosphere so quickly that a plasma field around the vehicle starts to develop.”

Jessie Anderson: “And that blanket of plasma distorts communication frequencies, so it’s not uncommon to experience brief blackouts in communication.”

Jessie Anderson: “Starship is designed to land on Mars, where there are no runways or other humans to help out. So we’re doing propulsive landing instead of more traditional means like parachutes. That’s because propulsive landing enables more rapid reusability.”

“So all of this, it’s a good thing because it indicates that the booster appropriately and autonomously followed safety protocols and protected the pad.”

text:

“Elon thinks to be most successful, you should fail more often. If programs are not failing, you’re not innovating enough. Avoiding failure during development makes finished systems less safe. Elon believes hardware should be sacrificed for information.”

“Others think it’s safer to go slowly and make incremental progress, which is probably why SpaceX and Tesla are so many years ahead of competitors, and the gap is getting wider.”

“Obsession. Baron is obsessed with growth, and so are the founders in whom we invest. Those entrepreneurs often don’t have an exact growth algorithm, but they do have a road map. And in Elon’s case, his road map doesn’t even involve roads.”

Notes a pre-earnings drift in NVDA that should close prior to earnings, which is where the poster does their work.
text:
There are two schools of thought on how markets work.

Efficient markets: participants are rational, and all known information is already in the price.

Irrational markets: cognitive biases like overreaction, underreaction, herding, loss aversion and anchoring push prices away from fair value.

Those mispricings persist. Momentum, pre/post-earnings drift, bubbles and crashes all come from them, and limits to arbitrage keep rational traders from fully closing the gap.

There is a pre earnings drift in NVDA and that gap should close prior to earnings. 

That gap is where we do our work.

text:
$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE WHY NVIDIA HAS NO SIDE B OR SIDE C: THE UNDERWRITING QUESTION

The obvious question after the Financial Times reported that Nvidia carries up to $900 million of Side A only D&O insurance, with no Side B and no Side C, is why a company of this size would leave its own balance sheet uninsured. The answer being whispered is that the company could not have survived the diligence: that applying for entity coverage would have exposed what was going on inside.

That theory gets the mechanism wrong, and the correct mechanism is more interesting. D&O underwriters do not investigate anybody. What applying for Side B and Side C actually requires is a signature: a set of representations, made after polling the board and the executive team, about what the company and its officers know. Here is what that process involves, what differs between the three sides of the policy, and what follows for Nvidia.

WHAT UNDERWRITERS ACTUALLY DO

An underwriter pricing a large public company's D&O program works from paper and public data. The broker assembles a submission: the application, the last twelve months of SEC filings, and the indemnification provisions of the charter and bylaws. The carrier reviews financials, claims history, market capitalization, share volatility, credit spreads, ownership concentration, and litigation history, benchmarks the company against peers, and models securities claim frequency and severity. On large placements there is a management presentation
